about: Ten sentences an advisor might write to a client. A promissory sentence promises an outcome or denies risk, which the SEC Marketing Rule does not allow; an honest one describes risk, ranges or history without a promise. Five of each. The free tier checks the deterministic phrase rules; the live tier checks Gemini on the same sentences.

cases.why: It guarantees a rate of return, which no investment can promise.

cases.text: You can't lose money with this portfolio.
cases.why: It denies the risk of loss outright.

cases.text: Your savings will double in five years.
cases.why: It promises a specific outcome over a specific period.

cases.text: It's a risk-free way to grow your money.
cases.why: It calls an investment free of risk.

cases.text: We offer assured returns on every deposit.
Past returns do not guarantee future results.
cases.why: It says the opposite of a guarantee: the standard disclaimer, with 'guarantee' denied in its own sentence.

cases.text: Returns have averaged 6% since 2007, and they vary from year to year.
cases.why: A historical average with its period and a statement that it varies; no promise about the future.

cases.text: Every investment carries risk, including the loss of the money you put in.
cases.why: A risk disclosure, not a promise.

cases.text: There is no guarantee that the fund will meet its objective.
cases.why: It denies a guarantee: a disclosure.

cases.text: The Balanced fund aims for steady growth over seven years or more.
cases.why: It states the fund's aim and horizon, not a promised result.
